answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ is the only place we found that pins this line to a document: it cites Why We Win by Billy Packer and Roland Lazenby (Masters Press, 1999), page 15. That edition is real — the Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗ gives Masters Press, Lincolnwood, Illinois — but the scan is lending-restricted, so we could not read page 15 and cannot confirm the wording sits on it. Quote Investigator ↗ has not examined the line, and no earlier printing surfaced. We therefore record it as attributed: well-anchored to a specific book by the specialist we defer to, and not independently confirmed by us.

trail: Wikiquote’s Red Auerbach page ↗ carries this as the only quotation attributed to Auerbach himself, and it is the only one on the page with a book citation: Billy Packer & Roland Lazenby, Why We Win, Masters Press, 1999, p. 15. Under this pipeline’s rules Wikiquote’s sourced section is the anchor we defer to, and we do not assert anything beyond what it documents — which is why no page-level confirmation is claimed here.

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for Why We Win ↗ independently confirms the edition behind that citation: Why we win: great American coaches offer their strategies for success in sports and life, Masters Press, Lincolnwood, Illinois, 1999. Confirming the book exists is not the same as confirming the sentence is on page 15, and the lending restriction stopped us there.

Wikipedia’s article on Red Auerbach ↗ establishes the man the line is about: an American basketball coach and executive who took the Celtics to eight consecutive NBA championships between 1959 and 1966, held an NBA coaching record of 938 wins on retiring in 1966, served as general manager from 1966 to 1984, and won sixteen NBA titles across his career.

author.bio: Arnold Jacob “Red” Auerbach was an American professional basketball coach and executive, and the architect of the Boston Celtics. As head coach he led the team to eight consecutive NBA championships between 1959 and 1966, retiring in 1966 with an NBA coaching record of 938 wins. He then ran the franchise as general manager from 1966 to 1984 and later as president and vice-chairman of the board, collecting sixteen NBA titles in all.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Auerbach ran the most successful dynasty in American team sport — eight straight NBA championships from 1959 to 1966 ↗ and sixteen titles in all — and the line is a compressed statement of the method. “Handling” is what you do to something that cannot argue back. His claim is that the moment a coach starts handling players, he has stopped coaching them.

It reads as a management aphorism now, which is how it travels: the distinction between the two verbs is doing all the work, and it survives being lifted out of whatever conversation produced it. That portability is also why its origin is hard to trace.
